query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermo-oxidative surface treatment that pre-forms an adherent nanocomposite oxide-rich tribolayer on high-entropy alloy surfaces will reduce both the coefficient of friction and wear rate across a broad temperature range (from ambient to ~800 °C) compared to untreated alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Untreated high-entropy alloy with its native surface structure and minimal pre-formed oxide layer.
generation.intervention: A single-step, controlled pre-oxidation (thermo-oxidative surface treatment) performed in a low-oxygen atmosphere designed to generate a 1–5 μm thick, nanocomposite oxide-rich tribolayer.
generation.conditions: Mechanical sliding contact under service temperatures ranging from ambient up to approximately 800 °C; the treatment is applied prior to operation so that the tribolayer persists and maintains ductility and lubricity under variable thermal loads.
generation.structural_mediator: An engineered, adherent, nanocomposite oxide-rich tribolayer consisting of multiple metal oxides that is sufficiently robust to withstand mechanical shear and resist spallation across a wide temperature range.
generation.mechanism: The pre-formed oxide layer acts as a lubricious, self-healing boundary that can shear easily during sliding contact, thereby reducing friction. Its nanocomposite nature bridges the gap between ductility and hardness, minimizing wear by resisting crack propagation and delamination, even as operating temperature increases.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the treated sample is predicted to exhibit a significantly reduced coefficient of friction and lower wear rates across low to high temperatures, with improvements potentially on the order of 20% or more, though the precise magnitude is uncertain.
generation.baseline: Untreated high-entropy alloy surfaces that rely on in situ formation of tribofilms under sliding, which may be less consistent over a broad temperature range.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the thermo-oxidative layer is expected to sustain under mechanical loading conditions typical for self-lubricating moving components, but may break down under excessively high loads beyond the tested regime or if the treatment parameters (time, temperature, oxygen partial pressure) deviate significantly from the optimized conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in friction and wear metrics, and the long-term stability of the oxide layer across repeated thermal cycling, remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one set that undergoes the controlled thermo-oxidative surface treatment and a control set that remains untreated. Subject both sets to sliding wear experiments under controlled loads at multiple temperatures (ambient, intermediate ~400 °C, and high ~800 °C). Monitor friction coefficients and wear rates over repeated cycles.
measurements: Wear rate via profilometry and mass loss measurements
Surface composition and layer integrity via SEM/EDS and XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction (e.g., at least 20% improvement) in both friction coefficient and wear rate in at least two of the three tested temperature regimes compared to the untreated samples, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

Wear-related energy and material loss cost over 2500 Billion Euro per year. Traditional wisdom suggests that high-strength materials reveal low wear rates, yet, their plastic deformation mechanisms also influence their wear performance. High strength and homogeneous deformation behavior, which allow accommodating plastic strain without cracking or localized brittle fracture, are crucial for developing wear-resistant metals. Here, we present an approach to achieve superior wear resistance via in-situ formation of a strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surface during wear, by reaction of the metal surface with its oxidative environment, a principle that we refer to as ‘reactive wear protection’. We design a TiNbZr-Ag alloy that forms an amorphous-crystalline oxidic nanocomposite surface layer upon dry sliding. The strong (2.4 GPa yield strength) and deformable (homogeneous deformation to 20% strain) nanocomposite surface reduces the wear rate of the TiNbZr-Ag alloy by an order of magnitude. Both sliding speed and normal load will affect the friction and wear behavior of the different grain size CoCrFeMnNi HEAs. Increasing the sliding speed will increase the friction coefficient and specific wear rate of the alloy. Thus, increase the normal load, reduce the friction coefficient, and decrease the specific wear rate of the alloy. This is because the oxide layer formed on the worn surface under high load plays a role in lubrication and reduces the friction coefficient and specific wear rate.

decision.trend: Early work on high-entropy alloys (HEAs) for friction and wear focused on exploiting near-surface structural transformations (e.g., tribo-induced nanocrystallization or amorphization) to reduce friction, mainly at ambient or specialized conditions (PMC7311485, PMC8448869). More recent efforts extended the temperature range; a key example demonstrated ultralow wear rates and stable tribofilms up to 800 °C using a nanohierarchical architecture and composition undulation (PMC10241162). In parallel, self-lubricating 2D HEA nanoflakes leveraged tribocatalytic activity to maintain very low friction and wear in ambient conditions under high contact pressures (PMC12019924). Despite these advances, achieving a single, steady, self-lubricating mechanism that remains effective from low to elevated temperatures—with no composition changes introduced into the alloy—continues to pose a major challenge.
decision.unsolved: A major open problem remains how to stabilize lubricious films so that they form and persist across widely varying temperatures without requiring an extensive redesign of the base alloy or repeated lubricant reapplication. While novel tribocatalytic surface layers and in situ oxide-scale formation can dramatically reduce friction, there is no single, standardized approach that ensures reliable self-lubrication for HEAs spanning from ambient to high temperatures in mechanically demanding environments.
decision.lever: A thermo-oxidative surface treatment to form an adherent nanocomposite oxide-rich tribolayer (approx. 1–5 μm thick), designed to remain ductile and lubricious from ambient to ~800 °C. The layer forms by controlled pre-oxidation in a low-oxygen-carrier environment, yielding an oxide constituted of multiple cation species that fosters easy shearing and resists brittle spallation.
decision.why: Reactive oxide-based films have proven beneficial for wear reduction and self-healing under friction (PMC8448869). Combined with the temperature-spanning success of nanohierarchical HEAs (PMC10241162) and evidence of self-lubricating action in tribo-catalytic HEA coatings (PMC12019924), a carefully optimized, single-step surface oxidation could yield a stand-alone engineered film that consistently cuts friction and wear under mechanical loads from ambient up to high temperatures.
